cards.front: What do a solid red light, a red arrow and a flashing red light each require?
cards.back: Yield at controls to priority holders; solid red means stop with right turns allowed unless banned after stopping and yielding, red arrows ban turns till green, flashing red means stop-then-go.

cards.front: How do a solid red, a red arrow and a flashing red differ?
cards.back: Solid red allows right turns after stopping unless banned, red arrows ban every turn until green, and flashing red behaves like a stop sign with movement after stopping, while all three still yield to right-of-way holders.

cards.front: What does a solid yellow light warn of, and what do yellow arrows mean?
cards.back: Solid yellow warns of red ahead: stop when safe, else cross carefully; yellow arrows end protected turns, and committed drivers finish, watching the next signal.

cards.front: What do flashing yellow, flashing arrows, green, green arrows and dark signals mean?
cards.back: Flashing yellow means slow without stopping, flashing arrows allow yielded turns, green means go while yielding inside with exit room, green arrows protect, dead signals mean all-way stops.

cards.front: How do flashing yellow, flashing yellow arrows, green arrows and dark signals compare?
cards.back: Flashing yellow needs no stop unlike flashing red, flashing yellow arrows leave the turn unprotected unlike green arrows, green still demands yielding to trapped traffic and exit room, and dark signals default to all-way stops.

cards.front: What do WALK, DON'T WALK, flashing DON'T WALK, countdowns and diagonal walks mean?
cards.back: WALK means cross, DON'T WALK means wait, flashing DON'T WALK means hold back, drivers still yielding; countdowns time crossings, diagonal walks allow any direction, sounds guide the blind.

cards.front: What do STOP signs and YIELD signs each demand?
cards.back: STOP signs demand full stops at the crosswalk, line, or entry, checking all ways; red YIELD signs demand slowing, ready to stop for all traffic.

cards.front: How do the DON'T WALK signals and STOP versus YIELD signs differ?
cards.back: Steady DON'T WALK forbids crossing while flashing DON'T WALK forbids starting with drivers still yielding, countdowns and diagonal walks refine timing and direction, and STOP signs demand full stops where red YIELD signs demand only readiness.

cards.front: What do red-and-white signs and white signs tell you?
cards.back: Red-and-white signs ban moves like U-turns and turns, white signs post no parking, one way, do not block, plus construction, guide, hazmat, slow-vehicle art.

cards.front: What color split separates bans from standing rules?
cards.back: Red-and-white signs prohibit maneuvers while white signs post standing rules, a color split that separates bans from standing orders across the regulatory gallery.

cards.front: What do yellow warning signs preview?
cards.back: Yellow warnings preview wet slipperiness, merging traffic, divided-highway shifts, two-way traffic, ending lanes, signals ahead, crossings, added lanes, crossroads, stop or yield ahead, curves, windings.

cards.front: Do yellow diamond signs give orders?
cards.back: Yellow diamonds warn of conditions rather than ordering action, previewing curves, merges, crossings, and controls ahead instead of commanding stops or bans.

cards.front: What should you do at a WRONG WAY sign, and what do sign shapes mean?
cards.back: Obey red-and-white orders like DO NOT ENTER, retreat from WRONG WAY signs, red night reflectors confirming; yellow-black circles and Xes mark rail crossings, pentagons schools, diamonds dangers, rectangles rules.

cards.front: How do the wrong-way signs work together, and what do the sign shapes code?
cards.back: DO NOT ENTER and WRONG WAY pair as the wrong-way system with red night reflectors as backup proof, while shape codes split meaning: circles and Xes for rails, pentagons for schools, diamonds for dangers, rectangles for rules.

cards.front: Who owns the right-of-way at an intersection, and when must you give it up?
cards.back: First arrival owns the right-of-way while the rest wait; never assume it; surrender it to stop crashes, scan unsigned crossings fully, always honoring pedestrians.

cards.front: How are ties, all-way stops, T junctions and turns settled?
cards.back: Unsigned ties defer right, all-way stops matching after stopping, T junctions favor the through road, lefts yield to pedestrians and close traffic, rights scan crossers, and blocking crossings with no exit room is illegal.

cards.front: How does first arrival relate to the right-side tiebreak?
cards.back: First arrival beats the right-side tiebreak which only fires on simultaneous arrival, all-way stops convert to the same tiebreak after stopping, T junctions exempt the through road entirely, and turns split duties between yielding lefts and scanning rights.

cards.front: How do you drive through a roundabout?
cards.back: Roundabouts circle one way: slow, yield inside, enter right into gaps, go counterclockwise, no stops or passes, signal exits, loop on a miss; multi-lane rights keep right, straights exit as entered.

cards.front: How do roundabouts differ from normal intersections?
cards.back: Roundabouts replace signal obedience with yield-on-entry and counterclockwise circulation, multi-lane rings assigning rights to the right lane while straights keep their entry lane, unlike normal intersections where lane discipline follows arrows and signs.

cards.front: Who counts as a pedestrian, and what must drivers do at crossings?
cards.back: Walkers, skaters, boarders, and disabled riders count as pedestrians yet obey road rules; drivers slow for crossers, never pass stopped cars at crossings, read eye contact as a cue; all crosswalks grant priority with stops at the limit line.

cards.front: Who counts as a pedestrian, and do unmarked crossings carry priority?
cards.back: Pedestrian status spans walkers to wheelchair riders yet binds them to road rules, driver duties escalate from slowing to full stops with eye contact as the cue, and unmarked crossings carry the same priority as painted ones.

cards.front: What priority do blind pedestrians have, and who yields on a steep pass?
cards.back: Blind pedestrians with dogs or canes always hold priority and wave drivers on, cane stowed; steep passes favor uphill vehicles, downhill ones reversing.

cards.front: What are truck No Zones, and how do car and truck stopping distances compare?
cards.back: Trucks hide cars in No Zones, so hidden mirrors mean you are hidden; braking grows with weight and speed, cars at fifty-five stopping inside three hundred feet, loaded trucks four hundred.

cards.front: What links blind pedestrians, mountain grades and truck blindness?
cards.back: Blind pedestrians hold unconditional priority with the stowed cane as the release signal, mountain passes trade on grade direction with downhill reversing, and truck blindness is mutual: hidden mirrors mean a hidden car.

cards.front: How should you treat long vehicles, safety zones and stopped transit?
cards.back: Long vehicles swing wide, so read their signals before passing; on wide divided roads they keep the two rightmost lanes, drivers never cut in, never linger, safety zones stay undriven, stopped transit passes at ten.

cards.front: How should you handle wide loads, safety zones and stopped transit?
cards.back: Wide-load maneuvering inverts car instincts: read the truck's signals before passing, expect the two-rightmost-lane rule on wide divided roads, and treat safety zones as absolute no-drive areas with ten as the transit-passing ceiling.

cards.front: When may you pass rail vehicles on the left, and how does light rail behave?
cards.back: Never pass rail vehicles or streetcars left except past right-hugging tracks, on one-ways, by officer order; light rail shares road rights, hides behind obstacles, preempts signals, never to be cut off.

cards.front: How should you share the road with motorcycles?
cards.back: Motorcycles share full road rights; drivers check mirrors and blind spots, hold three seconds, grant the whole lane, never pass in-lane, check before opening doors, shift aside.

cards.front: How do rail passing rules and motorcycle space differ from normal habits?
cards.back: Left-side passing of rail vehicles is banned with only three exceptions against the normal left-passing default, light rail preempts signals unlike ordinary traffic, and motorcycles demand full-lane generosity with three-second gaps and no in-lane passes.

cards.front: What must you do for emergency vehicles?
cards.back: Emergency vehicles with sirens and lights own the right-of-way: pull right and stop, move over for flashers, clear intersections, obey officers over signs, never trail within three hundred feet; slow triangular rigs get room.

cards.front: How does the response to sirens differ from the response to stationary flashers?
cards.back: Sirens plus lights trigger pull-right-and-stop while stationary flashers trigger move-over-and-slow, intersection presence means clear-first-then-stop, officer orders override every sign, and the three-hundred-foot trailing ban has no grace distance.

cards.front: How do slow vehicles, horse-drawn traffic and cyclists share the road?
cards.back: Scooters, neighborhood electrics, golf carts share roads slowly, NEVs capped at twenty-five and barred past thirty-five; horse-drawn traffic shares lanes, scaring banned; cyclists hold full rights: freeway stretches lacking alternates, hazard dodges, crosswalk use.

cards.front: What limits apply to neighborhood electric vehicles, horse traffic and cyclists?
cards.back: NEVs pair a twenty-five cap with a thirty-five road bar, horse traffic pairs shared lanes with anti-scaring law, and cyclist rights pair freeway access without alternates against hazard-dodge and crosswalk options.

cards.front: What must cyclists do, and what gear does a bike need at night?
cards.back: Cyclists obey signs, ride with traffic, shoulder-check, yield to pedestrians, helmet up under eighteen, stay visible and right, signal, brake well; night bikes carry a white lamp for three hundred feet, red rear light for five hundred, pedal and wheel reflectors.

cards.front: Where should slow cyclists ride, and when may they leave that spot?
cards.back: Slow riders hug the right curb except when passing, turning, dodging hazards, or narrowed out of sharing.

cards.front: How do cyclist duties and night gear compare with driver duties?
cards.back: Cyclist duties mirror driver duties with helmet, visibility, and right-edge extras, night gear triples into lamp, rear light, and reflectors with distance ratings, and the right-edge rule carries a full exception list for passing, turning, hazards, and narrow lanes.

cards.front: How should a driver pass a cyclist?
cards.back: Pass cyclists by changing lanes, or hold three feet when lane-locked, waiting otherwise; never squeeze riders, tuck behind before turning, enter bike lanes within two hundred feet, minding blind spots.

cards.front: What is the preferred order for passing a cyclist?
cards.back: Cyclist passing prefers a full lane change with the three-foot hold as fallback and waiting as the last resort, curbside merges and bike-lane entries staying conditional on safety and the two-hundred-foot turn window.

decks.module: Work zones, schools and rail crossings

cards.front: What do work zones demand, and what are the penalties?
cards.back: Work zones demand slowing, wider gaps, and full attention past cones and flaggers with early merges; violations cost one thousand-plus, fines double in enhanced or staffed zones, worker assault risks two thousand and a year inside, and drivers move over for amber-lit rigs.

cards.front: What does the work zone package include?
cards.back: Work zones stack slowing, gaps, attention, and early merges as a package, fines start at one thousand-plus and double under enhanced or staffed conditions, worker assault adds jail time, and amber-lit rigs command the same move-over as emergencies.

cards.front: Which trucks stop at rail tracks, and how should you handle bad weather and slow rigs?
cards.back: Diamond placards flag dangerous loads stopping before rail tracks; bad traffic and weather demand slowing without blocking flow, tow rigs and three-axle trucks live far right, yield right to faster followers.

cards.front: What is the school zone limit, and what should you watch for?
cards.back: School zones cap at twenty-five within five hundred feet of children, some at fifteen; scan for young cyclists, walkers, patrols, buses, reading yellow flashers as prepare-to-stop.

cards.front: How do placarded trucks, weather, slow rigs and school zones fit together?
cards.back: Placarded trucks stop at rails where ordinary trucks merely slow, weather slowing must not become flow blocking, tow and triple-axle rigs face lane confinement, and school zones pair the twenty-five cap with yellow-flasher warnings.

cards.front: What must you do when a school bus shows red flashers?
cards.back: Red bus flashers stop both directions till children cross and flashing ends, violators risking one thousand dollars and a year unlicensed, while buses across divided or multi-lane roads release the far side.

cards.front: What limits apply at blind intersections, alleys and rail crossings?
cards.back: Blind intersections, alleys cap at fifteen, rail crossings cap at fifteen where tracks hide past four hundred feet unless controlled, flashing reds forbid crossing till they end, warnings demand fifteen-foot stops, gates stay unducked, crossings need stop, look, listen.

cards.front: What do red bus flashers and the fifteen limit cover?
cards.back: Red bus flashers stop both directions with a thousand-dollar, year-long penalty tail while divided highways exempt the far side, and the fifteen cap triples across blind intersections, alleys, and hidden-track crossings with flashing reds and fifteen-foot stops layering rail obedience.

cards.front: What should you expect at rail tracks, and what is the district speed limit?
cards.back: Expect trains on any track anytime either way, never stop on rails, never enter without full exit room, and watch mandatory stoppers: buses, placarded trucks; business and residential zones cap at twenty-five unless posted.

cards.front: What is on the must-not list for drivers?
cards.back: No smoking with minors aboard, no animal dumping under fine and jail threat, no overloads, no cargo past the left fender, six inches right, no rear overhangs past four feet without a twelve-inch flag or two red night lights, no loose riders or video, no flaming litter.

cards.front: What rail behavior rules and prohibitions belong together?
cards.back: Rail behavior pairs never-stop-on-tracks with never-enter-without-exit-room and mandatory-stop watching, districts pair the twenty-five cap with posted overrides, and the must-not list pairs smoking, dumping, overloads, cargo limits, flags and lights, riders, video, and litter as one prohibition family.

cards.front: Where may windshield stickers go, and what rules cover processions and plates?
cards.back: Windshields stay clear save a seven-inch passenger square, five-inch driver square, five-inch toll square, rear side windows; marked funeral processions own priority, interruption ticketed, plates legible and unaltered.

cards.front: What are the penalties for fleeing police and for injurious reckless driving?
cards.back: Fleeing police by car means misdemeanor jail up to a year, pursuit injuries draw up to seven years, pursuit manslaughter four to ten, unlicensed use impounds your car thirty days, injurious reckless or contest driving draws jail, fines.

cards.front: What rules cover stickers, processions, plates and evasion penalties?
cards.back: Window stickers shrink to measured squares in fixed corners, funeral processions trade markings and headlights for priority, plates stay legible and stock, and evasion penalties staircase from misdemeanor jail through injury years to manslaughter decades with impound and contest penalties alongside.

cards.front: What happens if you skip court, and how many points trip negligent status?
cards.back: Skipped court dates suspend driving, marking the record, convictions persist thirty-six-plus months, adults trip negligent status at four in twelve, six in twenty-four, or eight in thirty-six months, one-point tickets trade once per eighteen months for insurer-hiding school.

cards.front: What follows point overload, and what forces revocation?
cards.back: Point overload brings probation, suspension, revocation, hearings, written notice, hit-and-run and injurious reckless driving force revocation, courts can suspend, and relicensing demands financial proof.

cards.front: How do court dates, convictions, points and overload fit together?
cards.back: Skipped court dates convert to suspension plus record marks, convictions linger thirty-six-plus months from any state, negligent status trips on the four-six-eight point staircase across twelve-twenty-four-thirty-six months, one-point tickets trade for school once per eighteen months, and overload ends in probation, suspension, or revocation with revocation forced for hit-and-run and injurious recklessness.

cards.front: What sanctions apply to provisional drivers and minors, and when do hearing requests lapse?
cards.back: Year-one provisional crashes, tickets bring restriction; minors draw action at one at-fault event, a thirty-day ban at two unless a licensed twenty-five-plus adult rides along, six-month suspension, year probation at three, year bans for substance convictions to age twenty; hearings lapse ten days post-service, fourteen post-mailing.

cards.front: How do provisional sanctions step up?
cards.back: Provisional sanctions staircase one event to action, two to a thirty-day ban with the licensed-adult exception, three to suspension plus probation, substances to year bans into age twenty, with eighteen erasing nothing; hearing rights lapse on the ten-fourteen day split.

cards.front: What rights do you have at a hearing, and what parts of records stay private?
cards.back: Hearings grant evidence, witnesses, testimony or counsel, cross-examination, with subpoenas on you against a documents-only case; unsafe drivers face reexamination, records public save conditions, addresses, social numbers.

cards.front: What does a hearing grant, and what stays private in records?
cards.back: Hearings grant the full defense toolkit against a documents-only case with subpoenas on the driver, unsafe drivers route through reexamination requests, and record privacy narrows to conditions, addresses, and social numbers.

recap_hooks.text: Solid red allows a right turn after stopping unless banned, red arrows forbid turns until green, and flashing red works like a stop sign.
Yellow warns of red, flashing yellow means slow, green arrows protect turns, dark signals are all-way stops, and STOP means a full stop while YIELD means be ready.
Red-and-white signs ban moves, white signs post standing rules, and yellow signs warn of conditions ahead.
Back away from WRONG WAY signs, and read shapes: circles and Xes for rails, pentagons for schools, diamonds for dangers.
First arrival goes first, ties go to the driver on the right, and T junctions favor the through road.
In a roundabout, yield on entry, go counterclockwise, never stop or pass, and signal your exit.
Pedestrians, including wheelchair riders, have priority at every crosswalk, and blind pedestrians always hold priority.
If you cannot see a truck's mirrors, the driver cannot see you, and loaded trucks need more distance to stop than cars.
Do not pass streetcars on the left except in listed cases, and give motorcycles a full lane and three seconds.
For sirens and lights, pull right and stop; for stationary flashers, move over; never follow within three hundred feet.
Neighborhood electric vehicles are capped at twenty-five and barred past thirty-five, and cyclists have full road rights and duties.
Slow riders keep right, and drivers pass them by changing lanes or keeping three feet.

recaps.module: Work zones, schools and rail crossings

recap_hooks.text: Work zones call for slowing and early merges, with fines that double in enhanced or staffed zones.
School zones cap at twenty-five, red bus flashers stop both directions, and blind intersections, alleys and hidden rail crossings cap at fifteen.
Expect a train any time, never stop on tracks, and know the must-not list.
Stickers go only in small set squares, processions have priority, and fleeing police brings jail time that grows with harm.
Skipped court dates suspend driving, and four, six or eight points in set months trip negligent status.
Provisional sanctions step up with each event, and hearings let you present evidence and witnesses.
